node.dia-daq-read.help: Reads samples from a data acquisition task on NI hardware, through NI's gRPC Device Server. The host the hardware is attached to needs NI's DAQmx driver and the NI gRPC Device Server, started with a configuration that turns on TLS, and with an address other than localhost if Flow runs on another machine. Never leave the server's unsecured port open on a plant network: set Security to on, or to mutual to also check this node's own certificate. Finite mode takes one acquisition of the samples you set on every call. Continuous mode starts the task on the first call and reads the next block of samples on each call after it. y is the samples of one channel as an array, or an array of arrays, one per channel in order. dt is the seconds between samples. A refusal from the server or the driver is an error on the error wire with the driver's own code and text. The task is cleared on the server when the run ends. This node has been tested against a stand-in server only, not against NI's server.

node.dia-filter.help: A Butterworth filter: flat in the band it passes, with no ripple, and 3 dB down at the cutoff. Lowpass keeps what is slower than the cutoff, highpass keeps what is faster, bandpass keeps what is between the two edges, and bandstop removes it. A higher order cuts off more sharply and rings a little longer after a step. The cutoff must be above zero and below half the sample rate. Give it an array, or one number at a time, and it remembers where it was between calls in a run, so a signal cut into pieces is filtered as one. The rate input wins over the Samples per second property. It starts from rest, so the first samples of an array carry a start-up settle; it delays the signal by an amount that depends on frequency, so it is wrong to use where the timing between two signals has to line up exactly; and it is not a linear-phase or zero-phase filter.

A refusal is an error on the error wire with the gate's own reason, and so is a HotLoop that cannot be reached; the write does not happen. A number is stored as a 64 bit float, a true or false as a bool, and anything else as text. A column that holds a list of numbers adds all of them, which is how a block of samples goes in. The properties are written on the file when the run starts. A file that already exists is appended to, so runs follow each other in one file, and a file cut short by a power loss is repaired to its last complete row before the new rows go on. With write to disk on, a power cut loses at most the row being written. It can start a new file when this one reaches a size or an age and keep only the newest finished files: bench.tdms becomes bench-20261114T120000Z.tdms and the log goes on in bench.tdms, with the file properties written again. node.dia-stable.help: Says whether the last readings agree. It keeps a window of the latest readings and is stable when the window is full and its highest and lowest differ by no more than the tolerance. An empty array, or one with anything that is not a finite number in it, is an error on the error wire.
node.dia-sub.help: A diagram used as a node. Its inputs and outputs are the connector: each input is a body in of that name in the body, each output a body out. node.exec.compat: The three outputs, both buffered and streaming modes, the timeout and the appended message property all behave as Node-RED's do. Two things do not, and neither is negotiable. There is no shell: the command line is split on quoting rules only, and an unquoted shell metacharacter is refused rather than run, so one allowed command cannot become an arbitrary one. And the node is disabled until an operator names the commands a flow may run. Node-RED's exec node runs anything, and Node-RED starts with no authentication by default; a vendor shipping that default became CVE-2025-41656 (Pilz IndustrialPI 4, VDE-2025-045), unauthenticated command execution on the device. Output is capped per stream; a command that exceeds it is killed and reported rather than being allowed to fill the heap. A command that forks children of its own may leave them behind when it is killed.
node.exec.help: Runs an external command and returns its stdout, stderr and exit status on three outputs. Disabled until the operator lists the commands a flow may run, and there is no shell, so quoting is the only thing interpreted in the command line.

node.function.compat: Runs on goja, a JavaScript interpreter written in Go, rather than Node's vm module. The language is ES2023; the Node standard library is not present. require() and npm modules do not work and cannot be made to without embedding Node. There is always a CPU time limit, which Node-RED leaves optional and off, and it applies to every timer callback too. setTimeout, setInterval and their clear functions work, on the node's clock, and every one is cleared when the flow stops or is redeployed. Buffer is there (alloc, from, concat, the read and write methods for integers and floats in both byte orders, slice, toString and toJSON). A byte slice in a message arrives as a byte array, so wrap it with Buffer.from.

HotLoop's own screens use the same feed. If the link drops the node says so on its badge and raises an error once, then keeps trying with a longer wait after each failure up to thirty seconds. When it is back, an entity that changed in the meantime is sent, and one that didn't isn't.

node.hotloop recipe.help:

HotLoop checks the whole recipe first and refuses it whole, writes every target in order through its write gate, and reads each value back from the device. The application is recorded under the account on the HotLoop connection with the reason flow:<node id>.

The message is sent on only when every target was written, with msg.payload set to the application, including whether each value was verified. A recipe HotLoop refuses, or one that stopped halfway, raises an error with HotLoop's reason, which names the target. Nothing that was written is undone.

The message is sent on with msg.payload set to the run: its status, its fields and, when the node waited, the trace of every step. node.http in.compat: Serves a path, with Express-style :params and a trailing *, and builds the same msg.req / msg.res / msg.payload shape Node-RED does, including JSON, form-encoded and raw bodies. Three deliberate differences. A request that no HTTP Response node answers is closed with 504 after a timeout instead of being held open forever, because Node-RED's version leaks a connection per request until the process runs out of sockets and stops answering with nothing in the log. Two nodes claiming the same method and path is refused at deploy time rather than one of them silently never firing. And a path that would shadow the editor or the admin API is refused for the same reason. Uploads parse the way multer does in Node-RED: text fields into msg.payload, files into msg.req.files, a broken upload answered with 500. One bound multer lacks: an array index over 10,000 in a field name, a[99999999], is refused instead of building a sparse array that long. msg.req.cookies is cookie-parser's, j: values included.

node.http request.compat: Method, URL, headers, basic authentication, redirects and the three return types, with msg.url, msg.method and msg.headers overriding the node. The response body is size-capped and the call is bounded by a timeout, neither of which Node-RED does. TLS comes from a tls-config, or without one msg.rejectUnauthorized = false skips the certificate check for that one message, as in Node-RED. msg.cookies and a cookie header go out through a cookie jar, cookies a redirect sets follow the redirect, and msg.responseCookies and msg.redirectList come back, all as in Node-RED. There is no egress allowlist: this node can reach anything the pod can, exactly as Node-RED's can, and the place to bound that is a NetworkPolicy rather than an edit dialog nobody outside the cluster can trust. networkInterface (not in Node-RED) binds the connections to one network interface.

node.watch.compat: Reports files and directories appearing, changing and being removed, with the same message shape Node-RED produces. It polls rather than using the kernel's notification interface, so a change is seen within the poll interval rather than immediately, and two changes inside one interval are reported once. That is a deliberate trade: fsnotify means per-platform code and a filename suffix that is a build constraint, which has already cost this codebase a day. Same path scope as the other file nodes, and the number of watched entries is capped so a recursive watch on a large tree cannot stall the runtime.

node.websocket out.compat: Replies to the connection named by msg._session, or broadcasts to every open connection when there is none, as Node-RED does. The divergence is what happens when a connection cannot keep up: the frame is refused to a Catch node and the connection is closed, rather than queued without limit. Blocking instead would push back-pressure from a slow browser into the flow's scheduler, which is a worse failure than losing a connection that had already stopped reading.

node.xml.compat: Both directions, using xml2js's object convention: attributes under the key named by "attr" (default $), element text under "chr" (default _), and every child element as an array, which is xml2js's own explicitArray default. Set ew_explicitArray to false to collapse single children instead. The per-message msg.options that Node-RED passes through to xml2js is not honoured — the other xml2js options change the shape of the output, and silently ignoring one would produce an object the flow does not expect while looking like it worked. Namespaces are kept as part of the element name rather than being resolved.
